charities.blurb: Funds pangolin research, rescue and anti-trafficking work across Asia and Africa.

name: African Bush Elephant
range: Savannas, grasslands and woodlands across sub-Saharan Africa
tagline: The largest animal that walks the Earth
lede: No land animal alive is bigger than the African bush elephant. A big bull can weigh as much as a city bus. Yet elephants are also among the most social and emotional animals on Earth, living in close families led by wise old females.
home: Bush elephants live across much of sub-Saharan Africa, from open savanna to woodland and even desert edges in Namibia and Mali. They travel long distances between water and food, and their old migration paths connect many national parks.
anatomy:
An elephant's trunk is a fusion of its nose and upper lip, with no bones, and is used for breathing, smelling, drinking, trumpeting, touching, grabbing and fighting. African elephants have two finger-like tips at the end of the trunk for picking up small objects.

The tusks are enormously enlarged incisor teeth that keep growing throughout life; both males and females of the bush elephant usually have them, and they are used for digging, stripping bark and fighting. Behind them, elephants have only four big grinding molars at a time, replaced from the back about six times over a lifetime.

Their huge ears are laced with blood vessels, and flapping them cools the blood. Their skin is up to 2.5 centimetres thick in places, wrinkled to hold moisture, and they protect it from sun and insects by spraying themselves with mud and dust.
life:
Elephants eat grasses, leaves, bark, roots and fruit, up to around 150 kilograms a day, and spend most of their waking hours feeding.

Herds are led by a matriarch, usually the oldest female, whose memory of water holes can mean survival in a drought. Males leave as teenagers.
family:
Elephant society is built around females. A herd is a family of related females and their young, led by the oldest matriarch, and several families may meet up in larger groups.

Females give birth after a pregnancy of about 22 months, the longest of any land mammal, usually to a single calf weighing around 100 kilograms. The calf can stand within an hour, and the whole family helps care for it: older sisters and aunts, called allomothers, guard, comfort and babysit it. Calves suckle for several years.

Young males leave the herd as teenagers and join loose groups of bulls. Adult bulls regularly enter a state called musth, when hormones surge, they become aggressive, and they search widely for females. Elephants grieve: they touch and stand over the bodies of dead relatives and return to their bones.
remarkable:
An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscles and can lift a log or pick up a single peanut.

Elephants talk in deep rumbles, many too low for us to hear, that travel kilometres through the air and ground. Their huge ears flap to release heat.
outlook:
African bush elephants are endangered. Poaching for ivory killed hundreds of thousands in recent decades, and growing farms and towns squeeze their habitat and cause conflict with people.

Where protection is strong, like in parts of Kenya and Botswana, numbers have recovered.
people:
Elephants have been revered, feared and hunted by people for thousands of years. Ivory was carved into art and ornaments across the world, and demand for it drove two great poaching waves, in the 1970s and 1980s and again after 2008, which killed hundreds of thousands of elephants.

In 1989 the international ivory trade was banned, and countries including China and the United States have since closed most of their domestic ivory markets. Today, elephants attract millions of tourists to national parks, supporting jobs and conservation funding.

As farms spread, conflict grows when elephants raid crops; communities in Kenya and elsewhere use fences hung with beehives, which elephants avoid, and chilli smoke to keep them out. Researchers fit elephants with GPS collars to understand their movements and protect corridors between parks.
relatives:
Three living elephant species are recognised: the African bush elephant, the smaller African forest elephant of Central and West African rainforests, and the Asian elephant. Forest elephants were long thought to be a subspecies, but genetics shows they separated from bush elephants millions of years ago. Elephants are the last survivors of the proboscideans, a group that once included woolly mammoths, mastodons and dwarf elephants on Mediterranean islands.

Surprisingly, their closest living relatives are manatees, dugongs and the small rabbit-like hyraxes, all part of a group of mammals that evolved in Africa. The earliest proboscideans, around 60 million years ago, were pig-sized animals without trunks. The woolly mammoth was more closely related to the Asian elephant than to African elephants.
didYouKnow: Research suggests elephants use distinct calls for individual family members, much like names.

quiz.prompt: Who usually leads an elephant herd?
choices: The biggest male, who fights off any challengers
Herds have no leader and simply follow the rains
quiz.explanation: A matriarch leads her family using decades of experience.

quiz.prompt: What is one purpose of an elephant's huge ears?
choices: Storing water for the long dry season
quiz.explanation: Flapping their ears helps elephants cool down in the African heat.

quiz.prompt: How do elephants communicate over long distances?
choices: Deep, low rumbles that travel kilometres
Flashing their tusks in the sun
quiz.explanation: Elephant rumbles, many below human hearing, carry far through air and ground.

charities.name: Save the Elephants
charities.blurb: Researches elephant behavior and works to end the ivory trade in Kenya and beyond.

name: Cheetah
range: Grasslands and savannas of eastern and southern Africa, plus a tiny population in Iran
tagline: Built for a few seconds of pure speed
lede: The cheetah is the fastest land animal on Earth, reaching about 100 km/h in a few seconds. Everything about it, from its slim body to its oversized heart and lungs, is designed for one explosive sprint.
home: Cheetahs need wide open country where they can see prey and chase it: grasslands, savannas and dry woodlands. Most live outside protected areas, on farmland in places like Namibia and Botswana, which makes good relations with farmers essential.
anatomy:
A cheetah is built more like a greyhound than a lion. It has a small, rounded head, a deep chest with large lungs and heart, a narrow waist and long, slender legs. Its spine is unusually flexible, bending and stretching with each stride so that, at full speed, the cheetah covers around 7 metres per stride.

Its enlarged nostrils and nasal passages take in plenty of air during a chase. Its short coat is pale gold with solid black spots, and its long tail, spotted near the base and ringed toward the tip, swings to counterbalance sharp turns.

The claws only partly retract and are blunt, like running spikes, but a sharp dewclaw on each front leg is used to trip and hold prey. Cheetahs have excellent eyesight, with a band of sensitive cells that lets them scan the horizon.
life:
Cheetahs hunt in daylight, often in the morning and late afternoon, to avoid lions and hyenas that hunt at night.

They stalk gazelles and impala, sprint, trip the prey with a paw, then must rest. Bigger predators often steal their kills, so they eat quickly.
family:
Female cheetahs live alone, except when raising cubs. After a pregnancy of about three months, a mother gives birth to around three to five cubs, in a hidden spot in tall grass or thickets.

The cubs have a long, silvery mane along their backs that may make them look like honey badgers, fierce animals predators avoid. The mother moves them often to keep them hidden, but lions and hyenas still kill many.

At about six weeks, cubs begin following their mother, and she brings them live prey to practise on. They stay with her for around 18 months. After they leave, brothers often stay together for life, forming groups called coalitions that hold territories and hunt together. Sisters soon split up and live on their own.
remarkable:
A cheetah's flexible spine works like a spring, and its claws only partly retract, gripping the ground like running spikes.

Its long tail acts as a rudder in sharp turns. The black 'tear lines' under its eyes may cut glare from the sun. Cheetahs can't roar, but they purr and chirp like birds.
outlook:
Fewer than about 7,000 adult cheetahs remain, mostly in southern and eastern Africa; the Asiatic cheetah in Iran is down to a handful.

Habitat loss, conflict with livestock farmers and illegal trade in cubs as pets are the main threats. Livestock guard dogs have reduced conflict in Namibia.
people:
Cheetahs have been tamed and used for hunting by royalty in Egypt, Persia and India for thousands of years. Akbar, the 16th-century Mughal emperor of India, is said to have kept a thousand.

That history contributed to their decline in Asia; the last cheetahs in India were shot in the 1940s, and from 2022 cheetahs from Namibia and South Africa were brought to India's Kuno National Park in an attempt to bring them back. In Africa, most cheetahs live on farmland, where farmers have shot them to protect livestock.

The Cheetah Conservation Fund in Namibia breeds large Anatolian shepherd guard dogs and gives them to farmers; the dogs scare cheetahs away, and farmers are far less likely to kill cheetahs. Cheetah cubs are also smuggled to the Middle East as pets, a trade conservationists are fighting.
relatives:
The cheetah is the only living member of the genus Acinonyx. It is not a big cat in the Panthera group; its closest relatives are the puma and the jaguarundi of the Americas.

This suggests that the cheetah's ancestors lived in North America and crossed into Asia and Africa. North America once had cheetah-like cats, in the genus Miracinonyx, that probably hunted pronghorns, which may explain why pronghorns are so fast today.

Modern cheetahs went through a severe population bottleneck around the end of the last ice age, about 10,000 years ago, leaving them with very low genetic diversity, which can affect their health and fertility. Several subspecies are recognised, including the critically endangered Asiatic cheetah of Iran. The rare 'king cheetah', with blotched stripes, is a pattern variation, not a separate species.
didYouKnow: A cheetah can go from standing still to about 95 km/h in only three seconds.

quiz.prompt: What may the black 'tear lines' on a cheetah's face do?
choices: Help it see in the dark at night
Show its age: they darken every year
quiz.explanation: The dark lines likely cut sun glare, helping cheetahs focus on prey in daylight.

quiz.prompt: Why do cheetahs' claws only partly retract?
choices: They grip the ground like running spikes
So they can dig dens for their cubs in hard ground
They're too big and thick to fit back into their sheaths
quiz.explanation: Semi-retractable claws give extra traction during high-speed chases.

quiz.prompt: Which sound can a cheetah NOT make?
quiz.explanation: Cheetahs purr, chirp and hiss, but cannot roar.

charities.name: Cheetah Conservation Fund
charities.blurb: Works with farmers in Namibia, including breeding livestock guard dogs, to protect wild cheetahs.

name: Okapi
range: Dense rainforest of the northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
tagline: The forest giraffe with zebra legs
lede: With striped legs like a zebra, a velvety chocolate coat and a face like a giraffe, the okapi looks assembled from spare parts. It was so secretive that Western scientists only described it in 1901, and it's still rarely seen in the wild.
home: Okapis live only in the dense rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, especially the Ituri Forest. The striped legs break up their outline in the dappled light of the forest floor, making them nearly invisible.
anatomy:
An okapi has a dark, velvety, reddish-brown coat that is oily and water-repellent, helping it stay dry in the rainforest. Its legs carry bold horizontal stripes of white and black, and its ankles are white.

Like a giraffe, it has a long neck relative to many hoofed animals, although nothing like a giraffe's, and males have two short, skin-covered horns called ossicones. Its tongue is dark and prehensile, around 35 centimetres long, used to strip leaves from branches.

Okapis have large ears that pick up quiet sounds, and their sense of hearing and smell are better than their eyesight in the dim forest. They have scent glands on their feet that leave a tar-like mark wherever they walk, helping them mark territories and find one another.
life:
Okapis are solitary browsers that eat leaves, buds, fruit and fungi, and they visit clay and charcoal from lightning-struck trees for minerals.

They follow regular paths through the forest. A mother hides her calf in a nest of leaves for weeks, and the calf barely makes a sound.
family:
Okapis are solitary and meet only to breed. After a pregnancy of around 14 to 15 months, a female gives birth to a single calf, which can stand within half an hour. Within days the calf goes into a nest in thick vegetation, where it spends most of its first two months hiding, emerging mostly to suckle.

During this time it barely needs to relieve itself, which keeps its hiding place free of scent that might attract leopards. Mothers communicate with their calves using very low-frequency sounds, possibly below the range that predators can hear well. The calf is weaned at about six months but stays near its mother for longer. Young okapis develop their full adult size over about three years.
remarkable:
The okapi's closest living relative is the giraffe. Like a giraffe, it has a long, dark, flexible tongue, long enough to clean its own eyelids and ears.

Okapis communicate with very low sounds that predators like leopards may not be able to hear.
outlook:
Okapis are endangered. Logging, mining and armed conflict in eastern Congo destroy their forest and make protection dangerous.

Rangers at the Okapi Wildlife Reserve protect them at great personal risk, and the okapi is a national symbol of the DRC.
people:
The okapi has always been known to the Mbuti and other peoples of the Ituri Forest. European explorers heard rumours of an 'African unicorn' and of a horse-like animal with stripes, and in 1901 British colonial official Harry Johnston obtained skin and skulls, leading to its scientific description.

It was named Okapia johnstoni after him. The okapi became a national symbol of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In 1992, the Okapi Wildlife Reserve was created in the Ituri Forest; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

During years of war and conflict in the region, rangers and conservation staff have faced violence, including a deadly attack on the reserve's headquarters in 2012, in which okapis at the breeding station were also killed. Conservation now includes supporting nearby communities with schools, healthcare and farming help.
relatives:
The okapi and the giraffes are the only living members of the family Giraffidae. Their lineages split roughly 11 to 12 million years ago, and the okapi is often called a living fossil because it resembles early giraffids, which had shorter necks.

Fossils show that the giraffe family was once far more varied, including Sivatherium, a massive, moose-like giraffid with broad ossicones, which lived until relatively recently in Africa and Asia. Giraffids belong to the even-toed hoofed mammals, along with deer, cattle, antelopes, pigs and hippos, and, more distantly, whales. Despite its zebra-like stripes, the okapi is not related to zebras, which are odd-toed hoofed mammals like horses and rhinos. Its stripes evolved as camouflage in the forest.
didYouKnow: Okapi stripes are thought to help calves follow their mothers through the dark forest.

quiz.prompt: What is the okapi's closest living relative?
quiz.explanation: Despite the zebra stripes, okapis belong to the giraffe family.

quiz.prompt: Where do wild okapis live?
choices: Rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
quiz.explanation: Okapis are found only in the rainforests of the DRC.

quiz.prompt: What can an okapi do with its long tongue?
choices: Clean its own ears and eyelids
Catch flying insects out of the air, like a chameleon
Breathe while wading through deep forest rivers
quiz.explanation: Its long, flexible tongue can reach its eyes and ears.

charities.name: Okapi Conservation Project
charities.blurb: Supports rangers and communities protecting the Okapi Wildlife Reserve.

name: Bornean Orangutan
range: Lowland rainforests and peat swamps of Borneo, in Indonesia and Malaysia
tagline: The thoughtful person of the forest
lede: 'Orangutan' comes from Malay words meaning 'person of the forest'. It's a fitting name. These great apes share about 97 percent of our DNA, use tools, and learn skills from their mothers over years of patient childhood.
home: Bornean orangutans live in rainforests and peat swamp forests on the island of Borneo. They are the largest tree-dwelling animals on Earth, moving slowly and carefully through the canopy and rarely coming down to the ground.
anatomy:
Bornean orangutans have long, shaggy, reddish-brown hair, very long arms that can span over 2 metres, and short, bowed legs. Their hands and feet are hook-like, with curved fingers and toes that grip branches, and their feet can grasp like hands. Adult males grow to roughly twice the weight of females.

Some develop large cheek pads called flanges and a big throat sac; these 'flanged' males dominate others and attract females. Other males may stay 'unflanged' for years, looking more like females, and only develop flanges later, often when a dominant male disappears.

Orangutans have excellent colour vision for spotting ripe fruit, and big, powerful jaws and teeth that can crack hard nuts and strip tough bark. They are the heaviest tree-dwelling animals, moving by climbing and swinging rather than jumping.
life:
Orangutans eat mostly fruit, especially figs and durian, along with leaves, bark, flowers and insects. Every evening, each orangutan bends and weaves branches into a fresh nest to sleep in.

Young orangutans stay with their mothers for about seven or eight years, the longest childhood of any animal except humans.
family:
Orangutans are the most solitary of the great apes. Adult males roam alone; females travel with their young. A female gives birth to a single baby after about eight and a half months, and the baby clings to her fur for its first year or more, nursing for up to six or seven years.

She carries it through the canopy, teaches it which of hundreds of plants are good to eat, how to build nests, and how to use tools. Young orangutans learn by watching and copying, and different orangutan populations have different traditions, a sign of culture.

Because a mother has a baby only every six to eight years, and females first give birth at around 15, an orangutan mother may raise only a few young in her lifetime, which makes populations very slow to recover from losses.
remarkable: Orangutans use sticks to pull seeds from spiky fruit and leaves as umbrellas, and they learn these tricks by watching. Adult males may grow large cheek pads called flanges and a throat sac that amplifies their 'long call', which can be heard a kilometre away.
outlook:
Bornean orangutans are critically endangered. More than half of the population was lost between 1999 and 2015, as forests were cleared for oil palm and paper plantations, burned in fires and logged.

Protected forests and rescue centres are helping, and choosing products with deforestation-free palm oil makes a difference.
people:
Orangutans feature in the folklore of the peoples of Borneo and Sumatra, and their likeness to humans has fascinated people for centuries. In the 1970s, scientist Biruté Galdikas began studying orangutans in Tanjung Puting, Borneo, and later founded Orangutan Foundation International; her decades of research, along with that of others, revealed much of what we know about their lives.

Logging, fires and the spread of palm oil and paper plantations have cleared huge areas of Borneo's forests, and orphaned orangutans are taken in by rescue centres, where they spend years at 'forest school' learning skills their mothers would have taught them before release. Shoppers can help by looking for products made with certified sustainable palm oil, and several governments and companies have pledged to stop deforestation in their supply chains.
relatives:
There are three orangutan species: the Bornean, the Sumatran, and the Tapanuli orangutan, described in 2017 from a small area of Sumatra and the rarest great ape on Earth, with fewer than 800 individuals. Bornean orangutans are divided into three subspecies in different parts of the island. Orangutans are great apes, along with gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans, and they are the only great apes living in Asia today.

Their lineage split from the African great apes around 14 to 16 million years ago. The largest ape that ever lived, Gigantopithecus, which lived in southern China until a few hundred thousand years ago and may have stood about 3 metres tall, was a close relative of orangutans.
didYouKnow: Because mothers have a baby only every six to eight years, orangutans are among the slowest-breeding mammals on Earth.

quiz.prompt: What does 'orangutan' mean?
choices: Red ape of the mountain forests
quiz.explanation: It comes from Malay words meaning 'person of the forest'.

quiz.prompt: How often do orangutans build a sleeping nest?
choices: Never; they sleep on the ground
quiz.explanation: Each evening they weave a new nest of branches high in the trees.

quiz.prompt: How long do young orangutans stay with their mothers?
quiz.explanation: Orangutans have one of the longest childhoods of any animal.

charities.name: Orangutan Foundation International
charities.blurb: Runs orangutan rescue, rehabilitation and forest protection in Borneo.

name: Platypus
range: Rivers and streams of eastern Australia and Tasmania
tagline: A mammal that lays eggs and hunts by electricity
lede: When the first platypus specimen reached Britain in 1799, some scientists thought it was a hoax: a duck's bill sewn onto a mammal. It's real, and the truth is stranger than the hoax. The platypus lays eggs, hunts with an electric sense, and the males are venomous.
home: Platypuses live in freshwater rivers, creeks and lakes in eastern Australia and Tasmania, from tropical Queensland to icy alpine streams. They dig burrows in the riverbanks with entrances just above the water line.
anatomy:
The platypus has a soft, rubbery, duck-like bill covered with tens of thousands of receptors: some sense touch, others detect the faint electric fields produced by the muscles of prey, letting it hunt in muddy water with its eyes closed.

Its body is streamlined and covered in thick, waterproof brown fur, so dense that it traps a layer of air that keeps the platypus warm in cold streams. Its front feet are webbed for swimming, and the webbing folds back when it walks or digs, exposing strong claws. The hind feet steer and act as brakes, and the broad tail stores fat.

Males have a hollow spur on each ankle connected to a venom gland, most active in the breeding season. Adults have no teeth; instead, hard pads in the bill grind food, along with gravel scooped up from the riverbed.
life:
Platypuses hunt at night for insect larvae, freshwater shrimp, worms and yabbies, eating around a fifth of their body weight a day. They store food in cheek pouches and grind it with rough pads, since adults have no teeth.

Females lay one to three eggs and nurse the babies with milk that seeps from their skin.
family:
Platypuses breed in late winter and spring. After mating in the water, the female digs a long nesting burrow in the riverbank, sometimes many metres long, and blocks the tunnel with soil plugs to guard against floods and predators. She lays one to three small, leathery eggs, about the size of a grape, and curls around them to keep them warm for around ten days.

The hatchlings are tiny, hairless and blind. Platypuses have no nipples: milk oozes from patches of skin on the mother's belly, and the babies lap it up. They stay in the burrow for three to four months before emerging to swim and learn to forage. Males play no part in raising young.
remarkable:
When a platypus dives, it closes its eyes, ears and nostrils. It finds prey using its soft bill, which is packed with sensors that detect the tiny electric fields made by muscles of moving animals.

Males have a venomous spur on each hind ankle, painful enough to disable a dog.
outlook: The platypus is listed as near threatened. Dams, drought, land clearing and pollution damage its rivers, and many drown in illegal 'opera house' yabby traps. Healthy, flowing streams with vegetated banks are what they need most.
people:
Aboriginal Australians have known the platypus for tens of thousands of years, and it appears in their stories; one tells of a platypus born from a duck and a water-rat. When a preserved platypus reached Britain in 1799, naturalist George Shaw reportedly checked for stitches, suspecting a hoax.

Scientists argued for decades over whether it really laid eggs, until this was confirmed in 1884. Platypus fur was once hunted for rugs, and hunting was banned in the early 1900s. Today the platypus appears on Australia's 20-cent coin and is a beloved national symbol.

Researchers and volunteers survey rivers using environmental DNA, collecting water samples and testing them for traces of platypus genes. Removing old 'opera house' yabby traps, which drown platypuses, and protecting stream banks are key to their future.
relatives:
The platypus is one of only five living monotremes, the egg-laying mammals; the others are four species of echidnas, spiny anteaters from Australia and New Guinea. Monotremes split from the ancestors of all other mammals, the marsupials and placental mammals, around 180 million years ago, so the platypus is a window into early mammal history.

Its genome, sequenced in 2008 and refined in 2021, mixes features of reptiles, birds and mammals. Fossil relatives show platypuses once lived in South America, and some extinct species had teeth as adults; one, Obdurodon tharalkooschild, was about a metre long. Young platypuses still grow small teeth, which they lose before leaving the burrow.
didYouKnow: Under ultraviolet light, platypus fur glows a blue-green color.

quiz.prompt: How does a platypus find prey with its eyes closed?
choices: It senses electric fields with its bill
It listens for the heartbeats of prey buried in the riverbed
It uses echolocation, clicking like a bat or dolphin
quiz.explanation: Electroreceptors in its bill detect the electric signals of moving prey.

quiz.prompt: How do platypuses have babies?
choices: Babies grow in a pouch from birth
They hatch from eggs laid by the father
quiz.explanation: The platypus is a monotreme, one of the few mammals that lay eggs.

quiz.prompt: What do male platypuses have?
choices: Venomous spurs on their hind ankles
Sharp teeth that they keep for their whole lives
A tail that gives off small electric shocks to stun prey
quiz.explanation: Males carry a venomous spur on each hind leg.

charities.name: WWF-Australia
charities.blurb: Works to protect Australian rivers, forests and the wildlife that depends on them.

name: Kākāpō
range: A few predator-free islands off New Zealand, such as Whenua Hou
tagline: A flightless parrot where every bird has a name
lede: The kākāpō is a moss-green parrot that can't fly, comes out at night, smells faintly of honey, and may live for decades. It is the heaviest parrot in the world, and one of the rarest birds on Earth. There are so few that every single one has a name.
home: Kākāpō once lived across New Zealand. Today they survive only on a few small islands cleared of rats, stoats and cats, such as Whenua Hou (Codfish Island) and Anchor Island, where rangers track every bird by radio.
anatomy:
The kākāpō is a large, round, moss-green parrot, mottled with black and yellow so it blends into the forest floor. It has a face framed by fine, whisker-like feathers, like an owl's, which may help it sense its way in the dark.

Its name means 'night parrot' in Māori. Its wings are short and its breastbone lacks the deep keel that anchors flight muscles, so it cannot fly, but it is a strong climber and a powerful walker, sometimes travelling several kilometres a night.

It stores large amounts of fat, which helps it survive lean times. Kākāpō have a strong, sweet, musty smell, which may help them find each other but also makes them easy for predators like stoats to find. Their sense of smell is unusually good for a bird.
life: Kākāpō eat leaves, seeds, roots and fruit, and they only breed in years when trees like the rimu produce a huge crop of fruit, which may happen only every two to four years. Instead of flying, they climb trees and use their wings like parachutes to glide down.
family:
Kākāpō breed only in years when certain trees, especially rimu, produce a huge crop of fruit, which may happen every two to four years. Males gather at traditional sites called leks, each digging a bowl in the ground and linking bowls with tracks.

Night after night for months, they inflate their chests and boom, a deep sound that carries far, followed by a high 'ching'. Females walk long distances to listen and choose a mate, then raise the chicks alone. A female lays one to four eggs in a nest on the ground.

She must leave the nest each night to feed, which once exposed eggs and chicks to predators. Chicks grow slowly and stay with their mother for months. Today rangers watch every nest with cameras and sometimes hand-rear chicks.
remarkable: To attract females, males dig bowl-shaped hollows on hilltops and inflate air sacs in their chests to make deep 'booming' calls that carry for kilometres, night after night. As a defense, kākāpō freeze when threatened, which worked against birds of prey but not against introduced mammals.
outlook: By 1995 only about 50 kākāpō were left. An intense recovery program, with island sanctuaries, supplementary feeding and veterinary care, has slowly lifted numbers to a couple of hundred. Each breeding season is followed closely across New Zealand.
people:
For Māori, the kākāpō was hunted for food and its feathers were woven into prized cloaks. After European settlement, introduced cats, rats and stoats devastated the birds, and by the 1970s the kākāpō was feared extinct, until small populations were found in Fiordland and on Stewart Island.

All surviving birds were moved to predator-free islands, and the Kākāpō Recovery program, run by the Department of Conservation with Ngāi Tahu, the iwi of the South Island, now cares for each one. Every bird is named, fitted with a transmitter and given health checks, and its genome has been sequenced to help plan matings.

A kākāpō called Sirocco, raised by people, became famous after a 2009 video and served as an official 'spokesbird' for New Zealand conservation. In 2020 the kākāpō was voted New Zealand's Bird of the Year, and again in 2008.
relatives:
The kākāpō belongs to a very old family of parrots found only in New Zealand, Strigopoidea, along with the kea, a clever mountain parrot famous for pulling apart cars, and the kākā, a forest parrot.

These parrots split from all other parrots tens of millions of years ago, possibly when New Zealand separated from the ancient supercontinent Gondwana. Without native land mammals to hunt them, New Zealand's birds evolved unusual ways of life: flightlessness, nesting on the ground and living a long time. The kākāpō is one example, along with the kiwi and the extinct moa.

Its long life and slow breeding were safe strategies until people arrived and brought predators. A fossil relative, Heracles inexpectatus, nicknamed 'Squawkzilla', was a giant parrot about a metre tall that lived around 19 million years ago.
didYouKnow: Kākāpō are thought to live for 60 years or more, one of the longest lifespans of any bird.

quiz.prompt: What makes the kākāpō unusual among parrots?
choices: It can't fly and is the heaviest parrot
quiz.explanation: It is the world's only flightless parrot and the heaviest.

quiz.prompt: How do male kākāpō attract mates?
choices: Deep booming calls from hollows they dig
Dancing to show off bright breeding feathers
Bringing gifts of fruit and seeds to the females' nests
quiz.explanation: Males boom from bowl-shaped hollows night after night.

quiz.prompt: What triggers a kākāpō breeding season?
choices: Years when rimu trees produce lots of fruit
Every spring, as soon as the days start getting longer
A full moon in the middle of the southern summer
quiz.explanation: They only breed in mast years when trees like rimu fruit heavily.

charities.blurb: New Zealand's Department of Conservation program that cares for every kākāpō.

name: Emperor Penguin
range: Sea ice around the coast of Antarctica
tagline: Raising chicks in the coldest place on Earth
lede: Emperor penguins do something no other animal attempts. They breed in the middle of the Antarctic winter, on sea ice, in temperatures that can fall below minus 40 degrees and winds of 150 km/h, in total darkness.
home: Emperors live around Antarctica, nesting in colonies on sea ice attached to the coast, sometimes far from open water. When they're not breeding, they hunt in the icy Southern Ocean, resting on floating ice between trips.
anatomy:
The emperor penguin is the largest penguin, with a black head and back, white belly, and golden-orange patches on the sides of its neck and the lower part of its bill.

Its feathers are short, stiff and packed tightly in several layers, with an underlayer of down, creating a windproof, waterproof coat. Beneath them lies a thick layer of fat. To save heat, emperors have small bills and flippers for their size, and blood vessels in their flippers, legs and nose that exchange heat, warming cold blood returning to the body. They can reduce blood flow to their feet to keep them just above freezing.

Their bodies are built for diving: solid bones, and the ability to slow their heart rate and redirect blood to vital organs. In water they are fast and agile; on ice they walk upright or slide on their bellies.
life:
Females lay a single egg and pass it to their mate, then walk back to the sea to feed.

For about two months, the male balances the egg on his feet under a warm flap of skin, eating nothing. Thousands of males huddle together, shuffling so each takes a turn in the warm middle.
family:
Emperor penguins gather at their breeding colonies in March and April, at the start of the Antarctic autumn, walking as far as 100 kilometres across the sea ice. Pairs find each other using distinctive calls.

In May or June, the female lays a single egg and carefully passes it to the male, who tucks it on his feet under a fold of skin called the brood pouch. She returns to the sea to feed, while males incubate through the darkest, coldest months, huddling in tight groups. The egg hatches after about 65 days. If the mother hasn't returned yet, the father feeds the chick a milky secretion from his throat.

When she returns, they swap, and the parents take turns making trips to the sea. Chicks gather in groups called crèches and leave the colony in December or January, as the ice breaks up.
remarkable: Emperors are the tallest and heaviest penguins and the deepest-diving birds: they can reach more than 500 metres and stay down for over 20 minutes. They survive the cold with dense feathers, thick fat, and a heat-exchange system in their legs and nose.
outlook: Emperor penguins depend on stable sea ice to raise their chicks. In recent years, early ice break-up has caused whole colonies to fail, and scientists project steep declines this century as Antarctica warms. Reducing greenhouse gases is the only real long-term protection.
people:
Emperor penguins live in one of the most remote places on Earth, and the first colony was not discovered until 1902, during Robert Falcon Scott's Discovery expedition. In the Antarctic winter of 1911, three members of Scott's later expedition made a gruelling journey through darkness and extreme cold to collect emperor eggs at Cape Crozier, a trip described in Apsley Cherry-Garrard's classic book 'The Worst Journey in the World'.

Today scientists monitor emperor colonies using satellite images, spotting the brown stains left by droppings on the ice from space. This technique has revealed new colonies and shown when colonies fail because sea ice breaks up too early. The emperor penguin was celebrated in films such as 'March of the Penguins', and in 2022 the United States listed it as threatened under its Endangered Species Act because of projected sea-ice loss.
relatives:
There are about 18 species of penguin, all in the Southern Hemisphere. The emperor's closest relative is the king penguin, which looks similar but is smaller, lives on subantarctic islands, and breeds in a different way, taking more than a year to raise a chick. Together they form the great penguins, genus Aptenodytes.

Penguins are related to albatrosses and petrels; their ancestors could fly, and penguins lost flight more than 60 million years ago, soon after the dinosaurs died out. Their wings became stiff flippers for swimming. Some ancient penguins were giants: Kumimanu, from New Zealand, may have weighed over 100 kilograms, and Palaeeudyptes klekowskii from Antarctica stood about 2 metres tall.
didYouKnow: A male emperor can lose almost half his body weight while incubating the egg through winter.

quiz.prompt: Who keeps the emperor penguin egg warm?
choices: The father, balancing it on his feet
The mother, in a nest of stones
quiz.explanation: Males incubate the egg on their feet for about two months.

quiz.prompt: When do emperor penguins breed?
choices: Only every five years, when the ice is thickest
Whenever the sea freezes far enough out from the coast
quiz.explanation: Emperors are the only penguins that breed through the Antarctic winter.

quiz.prompt: How do huddling males share warmth fairly?
choices: They shuffle so each takes a turn in the middle
The biggest stay in the middle
They take turns diving into the much warmer sea under the ice
They don't huddle; each keeps its own small space
quiz.explanation: The huddle slowly rotates so every penguin gets time in the warm centre.

charities.name: Antarctic and Southern Ocean Coalition
charities.blurb: Campaigns for marine protected areas and strong protection of Antarctica.

name: Polar Bear
range: Arctic sea ice and coasts of Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Norway and Russia
tagline: A bear that lives on the frozen sea
lede: The polar bear is the largest land carnivore on Earth, but it's really a creature of the sea ice. It is classified as a marine mammal, spends most of its life on frozen ocean, and can swim for days. About two-thirds of the world's polar bears live in Canada.
home:
Polar bears roam the sea ice of the Arctic Ocean and surrounding seas. In places like Hudson Bay, the ice melts every summer, forcing bears ashore to wait for freeze-up.

The town of Churchill, Manitoba, sees so many that it's called the polar bear capital of the world.
anatomy:
Polar bears have longer necks and narrower heads than other bears, a streamlined shape that helps when swimming and when reaching into seal holes. Their fur has two layers: a dense underfur and long, transparent guard hairs with hollow cores that scatter light, making the bear look white or cream.

Underneath, black skin absorbs heat, and a fat layer up to 10 centimetres thick provides insulation and buoyancy. Their huge front paws, up to 30 centimetres across, work as paddles in the water and spread their weight on thin ice; the soles are partly furred and covered with small bumps for grip.

Their claws are short, thick and curved for gripping ice and seizing prey. Polar bears have a superb sense of smell and can locate seals under snow, but they overheat easily when running, so they usually move slowly and save energy.
life:
Polar bears hunt seals, especially ringed and bearded seals, waiting patiently beside breathing holes in the ice or stalking seals resting on the surface.

A bear can smell a seal from more than a kilometre away. Pregnant females dig snow dens where tiny cubs are born in winter.
family:
Polar bears mate on the sea ice in spring. The fertilised egg doesn't implant until autumn, and only if the female has built up enough fat. She then digs a maternity den in a snowdrift, often on land, and gives birth in midwinter, usually to twins.

Cubs are born blind, with fine fur, weighing only around 600 grams. The family stays in the den for three to four months while the mother, who has not eaten since autumn, nurses them on milk that is very rich in fat.

In March or April they emerge, and the cubs follow their mother onto the sea ice, where she teaches them to hunt. Cubs stay with her for about two and a half years. Males play no part in raising cubs, and sometimes kill them.
remarkable:
Polar bears aren't really white. Their skin is black to soak up heat, and their fur is made of transparent, hollow-cored hairs that scatter light and look white.

A thick layer of fat keeps them warm even while swimming in icy water.
outlook:
Polar bears need sea ice to hunt, and Arctic sea ice is shrinking as the climate warms.

Longer ice-free seasons mean longer fasts and thinner bears, and some populations have already declined. Their future depends on how fast global emissions fall.
people:
Inuit have lived alongside polar bears for thousands of years. The bear, called nanuq, holds an important place in their culture and stories, and Inuit hunters still harvest a limited number under co-management agreements, using the meat and hides.

In 1973, the five countries with polar bears signed an agreement to protect them and their habitat, one of the first international wildlife treaties. Tourism has become important in Churchill, Manitoba, where visitors watch bears from tundra vehicles each autumn as they wait for Hudson Bay to freeze.

The town runs a polar bear alert program and even has a 'polar bear jail' where problem bears are held until the ice forms, then released. Scientists use collars, aerial surveys and even genetic sampling of footprints in the snow to monitor populations.
relatives:
Polar bears are closely related to brown bears, including grizzlies, and are thought to have evolved from brown bear ancestors living in the Arctic within the last few hundred thousand to around a million years, a short time in evolutionary terms. The two species can still interbreed, and wild hybrids, sometimes called 'pizzly' or 'grolar' bears, have been found in the Canadian Arctic as grizzlies move north.

Genetic studies show that brown bears on Alaska's ABC Islands carry polar bear DNA from past interbreeding. Bears as a family, Ursidae, include eight living species, from the sun bear to the giant panda, and are related to seals, sea lions and dogs. Polar bears are the most carnivorous bears, adapted to a diet of fat-rich seals.
didYouKnow: Polar bears have small bumps called papillae on their paw pads that grip the ice like non-slip soles.

quiz.prompt: What color is a polar bear's skin?
quiz.explanation: Black skin absorbs heat; the transparent fur only looks white.

quiz.prompt: What is the polar bear's main prey?
quiz.explanation: Ringed and bearded seals make up most of a polar bear's diet.

quiz.prompt: Why is sea ice so important to polar bears?
choices: It's their platform for hunting seals
They drink it as fresh water
It keeps them hidden from orcas
They sleep inside it all summer
quiz.explanation: Without sea ice, polar bears can't reach the seals they depend on.

charities.name: Polar Bears International
charities.blurb: Researches polar bears and the sea ice they need, based partly in Churchill, Manitoba.

name: Narwhal
range: Arctic waters of Canada, Greenland, Norway and Russia
tagline: The unicorn of the sea
lede: For centuries, Europeans sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns, worth more than their weight in gold. The truth is just as magical: a whale with a single spiralling tooth up to 3 metres long, living among the ice floes of the high Arctic.
home: Narwhals live year-round in Arctic waters, mostly in the Canadian Arctic and around Greenland. In summer they gather in ice-free bays and fjords; in winter they move offshore under thick pack ice, surfacing through cracks to breathe.
anatomy:
Narwhals are medium-sized toothed whales with a rounded head, small mouth and short flippers that curl up at the tips in older animals. Young narwhals are blue-grey; adults are mottled grey and white, and older ones become almost white. They have no dorsal fin, only a low ridge along the back.

Their famous tusk, usually found in males, grows from the left upper jaw and can reach about 3 metres. It spirals counterclockwise and is flexible, able to bend up to around 30 centimetres without breaking.

Its surface has many tiny channels leading to nerves inside, which has led scientists to suggest it may sense changes in the water. Narwhals have a thick layer of blubber and can slow their heart rate dramatically on deep dives. Like other toothed whales, they use clicks, whistles and buzzes to echolocate and communicate.
life: Narwhals travel in groups and eat Greenland halibut, Arctic cod, squid and shrimp, often swallowing prey whole by suction. They are some of the deepest-diving mammals, reaching more than 1,500 metres in winter to hunt in total darkness.
family:
Narwhals live in groups called pods, often of 10 to 20, though thousands may gather during summer migrations. Males sometimes rub or cross tusks, a behaviour called tusking that may help them size each other up. Mating happens in spring, offshore in the pack ice.

After a pregnancy of about 14 to 15 months, the female gives birth to a single calf, usually tail first, in summer. The calf is around 1.5 metres long and depends on its mother's rich milk for about 20 months, staying close to her side as the pod travels.

Females give birth roughly every three years. Narwhals mature slowly, at around 6 to 9 years, and can live for 50 years or more. Orcas, polar bears and being trapped in freezing sea ice are their main natural threats.
remarkable:
The tusk is actually a tooth, usually the left canine, that grows straight out through the upper lip in a left-handed spiral.

Most males have one; a few females do, and rarely a narwhal grows two. The tusk may be used to show off to rivals and to sense the water around it.
outlook:
Narwhals are currently listed as least concern, but they are very sensitive to change.

Melting sea ice opens the Arctic to shipping, noise and new predators like orcas, and their specialised diet makes it hard to adapt. Inuit communities hunt narwhal sustainably and help monitor them.
people:
Inuit have hunted narwhals for centuries for their skin and blubber, called muktuk, which is rich in vitamin C and an important traditional food, as well as for their tusks. Medieval European traders sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns, believed to cure poison; the Throne Chair of Denmark, made in the 1600s, is decorated with them.

Today narwhal hunting is managed with quotas in Canada and Greenland, often set by Inuit organisations and governments together. Scientists work with Inuit hunters, who know narwhal behaviour intimately, to tag the whales and study their migrations. As sea ice shrinks, more shipping, mining and seismic surveys reach the Arctic; their noise can disturb narwhals, so some communities have pushed for protected areas, such as Tallurutiup Imanga national marine conservation area in Nunavut.
relatives:
The narwhal's only close relative is the beluga, the white whale, and together they form the family Monodontidae. Belugas and narwhals share the Arctic, have no dorsal fin, and occasionally interbreed; a skull of a likely hybrid was found in Greenland in the 1990s. These whales are toothed whales, like dolphins, porpoises and sperm whales, which hunt using echolocation.

Fossils suggest that narwhal and beluga relatives once lived in warmer waters, such as the extinct Bohaskaia from Virginia and Denebola from Mexico, and that the family moved into the Arctic more recently. The spiral tusk is unique to the narwhal, and its evolution, from a normal tooth to a tusk that pierces the lip, still raises questions.
didYouKnow: Narwhals have no dorsal fin, which may help them swim under ice without scraping.

quiz.prompt: What is a narwhal's tusk?
quiz.explanation: The tusk is a tooth, usually the left canine, that grows through the lip.

quiz.prompt: Which narwhals usually have a tusk?
quiz.explanation: Most males grow a tusk; only a few females do.

quiz.prompt: How deep can narwhals dive?
choices: About 10 metres, staying near the surface to breathe
They stay in the top few metres of the sea
quiz.explanation: Narwhals are among the deepest-diving mammals in the ocean.

charities.name: WWF
charities.blurb: Works with Arctic communities to protect narwhals, sea ice habitat and marine life.

name: Blue Whale
range: All the world's oceans, from the Antarctic to the North Atlantic and Pacific
tagline: The largest animal that has ever lived
lede: Bigger than any dinosaur, the blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever existed. It can grow to around 30 metres long and weigh as much as 30 elephants. Its heart alone weighs around 180 kilograms.
home: Blue whales live in every ocean. Many travel between cold, food-rich feeding grounds near the poles and warmer waters where they give birth. Some populations, like one in the northern Indian Ocean, may stay in one region year-round.
anatomy:
A blue whale is long, slender and blue-grey, mottled with lighter patches. Under water it often looks bright blue. Its head is broad, flat and U-shaped from above, taking up nearly a quarter of its length.

Instead of teeth, it has hundreds of baleen plates, made of keratin, hanging from its upper jaw, fringed with bristles that act as a sieve. Up to about 90 grooves run from its throat to its belly; when it feeds, these pleats expand like an accordion so it can engulf a huge mouthful of water and krill.

Its blowhole spray rises up to 9 metres high. It has a small dorsal fin set far back on its body. Despite its size, a blue whale can reach speeds of around 30 km/h in short bursts and normally cruises much slower.
life:
Incredibly, the biggest animal on Earth eats one of the smallest: krill, tiny shrimp-like animals.

A blue whale lunges into a swarm with its mouth open, gulping a volume of water larger than its own body, then pushes it out through baleen plates that trap the krill. It can eat several tonnes a day.
family:
Blue whales are usually seen alone or in pairs, though they may gather where krill is plentiful. Little is known about their courtship. After a pregnancy of about 11 to 12 months, a female gives birth every two to three years, usually in warmer waters in winter. A newborn calf is around 7 metres long and weighs about 2.5 tonnes.

It drinks very rich, fatty milk and gains weight extremely fast, until it is weaned at around six to seven months, by which time it may be about 16 metres long. Mothers and calves often travel together during this time. Blue whales reach maturity at around 5 to 15 years. Calves are vulnerable to orca attacks, but adults have almost no natural predators.
remarkable: Blue whale calls are among the loudest sounds made by any animal, deep enough that much of it is below human hearing, and can travel hundreds of kilometres underwater. A newborn calf is about 7 metres long and gains around 90 kilograms a day on its mother's rich milk.
outlook: Whaling killed hundreds of thousands of blue whales in the 20th century, leaving some populations at a few percent of their original size. They have been protected since 1966 and are slowly recovering, but ship strikes, entanglement in fishing gear and ocean noise remain threats.
people:
Blue whales were too fast and powerful for early whalers, but the invention of the explosive harpoon and steam-powered whaling ships in the late 1800s made them targets. During the 20th century, especially in the Antarctic, whalers killed hundreds of thousands, and by the 1960s they were near extinction. The International Whaling Commission protected them worldwide in 1966.

Since then, some populations, such as those off California, have recovered substantially, while Antarctic blue whales remain a small fraction of their former numbers. Today, scientists use hydrophones to listen for their calls, satellite tags to follow them, and drones to measure their size and health.

Whale watching has become a valuable industry. Ships slowing down in key areas, as many do off California, and proposals to move shipping lanes off Sri Lanka aim to reduce deadly collisions with these giants.
relatives:
The blue whale is a rorqual, a group of baleen whales with throat pleats that includes the fin whale, sei whale, humpback whale and minke whales. The fin whale, the second-largest animal on Earth, is closely related, and blue and fin whales can interbreed. Several subspecies of blue whale are recognised, including the Antarctic blue whale, the largest, and the smaller pygmy blue whale of the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

Whales evolved from land mammals related to hippos around 50 million years ago, and baleen whales gradually replaced teeth with baleen. Large body size evolved quite recently, within the last few million years, perhaps as krill became more concentrated in seasonal hotspots, making huge size an advantage for filter feeding.
didYouKnow: Blue whales can live 80 to 90 years, which scientists estimate by counting layers in their earwax plugs, a bit like tree rings.

quiz.prompt: What does the blue whale mainly eat?
quiz.explanation: The largest animal on Earth survives on tiny shrimp-like krill.

quiz.prompt: How does a blue whale filter its food from the water?
choices: Through baleen plates in its mouth
With rows of small, sharp teeth
Through its blowhole, which works like a sieve
By straining water through its gills like a shark
quiz.explanation: Baleen plates trap krill while water is pushed out.

quiz.prompt: Since when have blue whales been protected from hunting?
quiz.explanation: Blue whales were protected internationally in 1966 after heavy whaling.

charities.name: Whale and Dolphin Conservation
charities.blurb: Fights threats to whales and dolphins, from whaling to ship strikes and entanglement.

name: Common Octopus
range: Coastal waters of the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic
tagline: Three hearts, blue blood and a brain in every arm
lede: The common octopus is about as alien as life on Earth gets: three hearts, blue blood, no bones, and skin that can change color in a fraction of a second. It's also remarkably clever, able to solve puzzles, open jars and escape from aquarium tanks.
home: Common octopuses live along rocky coasts, reefs and seagrass beds of the Mediterranean and the eastern Atlantic, usually in fairly shallow water. Each one makes a den in a crevice or shell pile, often decorated with the empty shells of its meals.
anatomy:
An octopus has a soft, rounded body called the mantle, a head with two large eyes, and eight muscular arms lined with suckers.

Each sucker can grip, taste and smell, and can move independently. The octopus has no bones; its only hard part is a parrot-like beak at the centre of its arms, so it can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak. It breathes with gills inside the mantle and moves by crawling or by jet propulsion, shooting water out of a tube called the siphon.

Its skin contains thousands of colour-changing cells called chromatophores, plus reflective cells and muscles that raise bumps and spikes, letting it change both colour and texture in an instant. Its eyes are sharp but probably cannot see colour as we do. It has a large brain for an invertebrate, wrapped around its oesophagus.
life:
Octopuses hunt mostly at dusk and night, catching crabs, clams and snails. They pry open shells or drill a hole and inject venom that softens the prey.

They live fast: most survive just one to two years. A female guards her eggs for weeks without eating, and dies soon after they hatch.
family:
Common octopuses live alone and are often cannibalistic, so mating can be risky. The male uses a specially modified arm, called the hectocotylus, to pass packets of sperm to the female, sometimes at arm's length. The female then finds a safe den and lays tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of tiny eggs, hanging them in long strings from the roof.

For weeks, sometimes months, depending on water temperature, she guards them without eating, blowing water over them to keep them clean and oxygenated and fending off predators. She dies soon after they hatch, and the male usually dies not long after mating. The hatchlings drift in the plankton for weeks, feeding on tiny animals, before settling on the seafloor. Very few survive.
remarkable:
About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, so each arm can taste, touch and react partly on its own.

Special skin cells change color and texture to match rock or seaweed instantly. When escape fails, it squirts a cloud of ink and jets away.
outlook: The common octopus is not considered threatened, but it is heavily fished, and scientists worry about plans to farm octopuses, given their intelligence and solitary nature. Several countries now recognise octopuses as sentient in animal-welfare law.
people:
Octopuses have been part of human cultures for thousands of years. Ancient Minoans painted them on pottery, and they appear in Japanese art, Greek cuisine and countless sea legends. Mediterranean fishers have long caught them in clay pots that octopuses use as dens. Scientists have been amazed by their intelligence: octopuses in aquariums have unscrewed jar lids, recognised individual keepers, squirted water at people they disliked, and escaped from tanks.

Researchers study their arms for ideas in soft robotics. In 2021, a UK government review found strong evidence that octopuses can feel pain and are sentient, and they were included in British animal welfare law. Proposals to farm octopuses for food have drawn criticism from scientists and animal welfare groups.
relatives:
The common octopus is a cephalopod, a group of molluscs that includes squid, cuttlefish and the nautilus. Cephalopods are relatives of snails and clams, though they lost or internalised their shells; the nautilus still has an external, chambered shell. There are around 300 octopus species, from the tiny star-sucker pygmy octopus to the giant Pacific octopus, which can have an arm span of several metres.

Scientists have recently realised that what was called the common octopus may include several closely related species around the world, and the name Octopus vulgaris is now often used only for populations in the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic. Octopuses evolved their large brains independently of vertebrates, making them a remarkable example of intelligence arising in a completely separate branch of life.
didYouKnow: An octopus's blood is blue because it uses copper-based hemocyanin to carry oxygen, instead of iron-based hemoglobin.

quiz.prompt: How many hearts does an octopus have?
quiz.explanation: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and one through the body.

quiz.prompt: Where are most of an octopus's neurons?
quiz.explanation: About two-thirds of its neurons are in its arms.

quiz.prompt: What happens to a mother octopus after her eggs hatch?
choices: She raises the young for a year
She lays another batch right away
She leaves to find a new den
quiz.explanation: Females guard their eggs without eating and die soon after they hatch.

charities.blurb: Campaigns to protect ocean habitats and end overfishing.

name: Leatherback Sea Turtle
range: Oceans worldwide, from tropical nesting beaches to the cold waters off Nova Scotia
tagline: The jellyfish hunter that crosses oceans
lede: The leatherback is the largest turtle on Earth and one of the great ocean wanderers. Instead of a hard shell, it wears a flexible, leathery carapace, and it travels thousands of kilometres from tropical beaches to cold northern seas, following the jellyfish it eats.
home: Leatherbacks have the widest range of any reptile. They nest on tropical beaches in places like Trinidad, Costa Rica and Gabon, then swim into cold waters, including off Nova Scotia and Newfoundland each summer, where jellyfish are plentiful.
anatomy:
The leatherback is the only sea turtle without a hard shell. Its back is covered by leathery, oily skin over a mosaic of thousands of small bones, shaped into seven long ridges that run from head to tail and help it glide through water.

It is usually dark grey or black, speckled with white, and has a pink spot on the top of its head that may be linked to sensing light and the seasons. Its front flippers are huge, spanning up to about 2.7 metres, and drive it across oceans.

Its mouth has sharp, tooth-like points on its upper jaw, and its throat is lined with backward-pointing spines that let water out while keeping jellyfish in. Its body can stay much warmer than cold water thanks to its size, fat insulation and a heat-exchange system in its flippers.
life:
Leatherbacks eat almost nothing but jellyfish, which are mostly water, so they must eat huge amounts.

Their mouths and throats are lined with backward-pointing spines that keep slippery jellyfish from escaping. Females come ashore at night to dig nests and lay dozens of eggs.
family:
Leatherbacks mate at sea, and females return to tropical beaches every two to three years to nest, often to the same region where they hatched.

On a nesting night, a female crawls up the beach, digs a deep hole with her hind flippers, and lays around 80 fertile eggs about the size of billiard balls, plus a layer of smaller, yolkless eggs whose purpose is still debated. She covers them and returns to the sea, and may nest several times in a season, about ten days apart.

The eggs incubate in the warm sand for about two months; as with other turtles, warmer sand produces more females. The hatchlings dig out together, usually at night, and race to the water, guided by the brighter horizon over the sea. Very few survive to adulthood.
remarkable: Unlike most reptiles, leatherbacks can keep their bodies warmer than the water around them, thanks to their large size, a thick layer of fat and clever blood vessels in their flippers. They can dive deeper than 1,000 metres, deeper than many whales.
outlook: Leatherbacks are vulnerable worldwide, and Pacific populations have crashed. They are often caught by accident in fishing gear, their eggs are taken, and they mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish. Beach protection and turtle-safe fishing gear are helping some Atlantic populations.
people:
Leatherback eggs have been collected for food in many places, and in some countries this is now illegal or strictly managed. Since the 1960s, conservation programs have protected nesting beaches in places such as Trinidad, Costa Rica, French Guiana and Gabon, often run by local communities who patrol beaches at night, guard nests and lead turtle-watching tours.

At sea, leatherbacks are often caught accidentally in fishing gear, so scientists have worked with fishers to develop changes like circle hooks and to close areas at key times. In Atlantic Canada, researchers have tagged leatherbacks feeding on jellyfish off Nova Scotia and found that some travel to nest in the Caribbean and South America. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches dark during nesting season and picking up plastic.
relatives:
The leatherback is the only living member of its family, Dermochelyidae, and it is very different from the six other sea turtle species, such as green, loggerhead and hawksbill turtles, all of which have hard shells.

Its lineage split from the other sea turtles over 100 million years ago. Fossil relatives in the same broad group include Archelon, the largest turtle ever known, which lived around 80 million years ago and was about 4.5 metres long. Sea turtles descended from turtles that lived on land, and they still breathe air and lay eggs on land, which ties them to beaches. Their reliance on beaches means that sea-level rise and coastal development are growing threats.
didYouKnow: Leatherback turtles have been around in some form for over 100 million years, since the age of dinosaurs.

quiz.prompt: What do leatherbacks mainly eat?
quiz.explanation: Leatherbacks live almost entirely on jellyfish.

quiz.prompt: How is a leatherback's shell different from other turtles'?
choices: It's flexible and leathery, not hard
It has no shell at all
quiz.explanation: Its carapace is leathery skin over small bones, not hard plates.

quiz.prompt: Why are plastic bags dangerous to leatherbacks?
choices: They look like jellyfish and get eaten
They scare away their mates during the breeding season
They change the temperature of the water near nesting beaches
quiz.explanation: Floating plastic bags are easily mistaken for jellyfish.
