charities.blurb: Protects nesting beaches and tracks sea turtles across the Atlantic and Caribbean.

name: Whale Shark
range: Warm tropical oceans worldwide, gathering at places like Ningaloo Reef and the Yucatán
tagline: The gentle giant with a starry back
lede: The whale shark is the biggest fish in the sea, as long as a bus, yet it's harmless to people. Swimmers who meet one see a vast, spotted body gliding slowly past, its wide mouth open, sieving the water for food far too small to see.
home: Whale sharks roam warm tropical oceans around the world, often far out at sea and deep underwater. At certain times of year they gather where food is plentiful: Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia, the Yucatán coast of Mexico, the Maldives and the Philippines.
anatomy:
The whale shark has a broad, flat head and a huge mouth at the very front of its snout, rather than underneath as in most sharks. Its dark grey to brownish body is covered with a pattern of pale spots and stripes, unique to each individual. Three prominent ridges run along each side of its back.

Its skin can be up to 10 centimetres thick, making it one of the thickest skins of any animal. It has five large gill slits on each side, and inside its mouth are filter pads that sieve tiny food from the water. It also has thousands of tiny teeth, which it does not use for feeding.

Scientists recently found that its eyes are protected by tiny tooth-like scales called denticles and that it can pull its eyeballs back into its head.
life:
Whale sharks are filter feeders. They eat plankton, krill, fish eggs and small fish, either swimming slowly with their mouth open or sucking in water while hanging upright.

Their gills have spongy filter pads that sieve out food. Much of their life, including where they give birth, is still a mystery.
family:
Very little is known about how whale sharks reproduce, as mating and birth have almost never been observed. In 1995, a pregnant female caught off Taiwan was found to be carrying about 300 developing young, at different stages, revealing that whale sharks hatch from eggs inside the mother and are born alive. Pups are born around 40 to 60 centimetres long.

Scientists believe whale sharks mature slowly; males may not mature until they are around 25 to 30 years old and 8 to 9 metres long. Young whale sharks are rarely seen, and it is still not known where most are born. Many of the gatherings at feeding sites, such as Ningaloo or the Maldives, are dominated by young males.
remarkable: Each whale shark's pattern of pale spots and stripes is unique, like a fingerprint. Researchers and divers photograph the spots behind the gills, and computer software originally designed to map stars matches them to identify individuals across years and oceans.
outlook:
Whale sharks are endangered. They grow and breed slowly, and numbers have fallen because of fishing, accidental catch in nets, and collisions with ships.

Well-managed tourism, like at Ningaloo, now makes a living whale shark far more valuable than a dead one.
people:
In some places whale sharks were once hunted for their meat, fins and oil, but many countries now protect them, and international trade is regulated under CITES, the treaty that governs the global wildlife trade. In Vietnam, fishers call the whale shark 'Ca Ong', Mr Fish, and treat it with respect.

Today, whale shark tourism supports local communities from Mexico and Belize to the Philippines and Western Australia; swimming alongside one is considered a bucket-list experience, and in places like Ningaloo strict guidelines limit how close swimmers get. Citizen science plays a large role in research: divers and tourists upload photos of the spots behind a shark's gills to global databases, where pattern-matching software originally developed for astronomers identifies individuals. These photo records have helped track thousands of whale sharks over years and across oceans.
relatives:
The whale shark is the only species in its family, Rhincodontidae. It belongs to the carpet sharks, an order that includes nurse sharks, zebra sharks and wobbegongs, which mostly live on the seafloor; the whale shark is the only one that lives in open water. Two other sharks are filter feeders: the basking shark, the second-largest fish, and the deep-sea megamouth shark, discovered only in 1976.

Each evolved filter feeding separately. Sharks have existed for more than 400 million years, longer than trees, and their skeletons are made of cartilage, not bone. The famous extinct giant shark megalodon, which reached perhaps 15 to 20 metres, was a predator, unlike the gentle whale shark.
didYouKnow: A whale shark's mouth can be more than a metre wide and contains thousands of tiny teeth that it doesn't use for eating.

quiz.prompt: What kind of animal is a whale shark?
choices: A fish, the largest in the sea
A whale that looks like a shark
A ray, closely related to the giant manta
quiz.explanation: Despite the name, it's a shark, and the world's biggest fish.

quiz.prompt: What does a whale shark eat?
choices: Plankton and tiny animals it filters from the water
quiz.explanation: It's a gentle filter feeder that sieves plankton and small prey.

quiz.prompt: How do researchers tell individual whale sharks apart?
choices: By their unique pattern of spots
By the shape and number of their teeth
By the songs they sing, which are unique to each one
By the colour of their eyes
quiz.explanation: Each spot pattern is unique, like a fingerprint.

charities.name: Marine Megafauna Foundation
charities.blurb: Researches and protects whale sharks, manta rays and other ocean giants.

name: Strawberry Poison Frog
range: Lowland rainforests of Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama
tagline: A tiny jewel that's a devoted parent
lede: Barely 2 centimetres long and bright as a candy, the strawberry poison frog is impossible to miss on the rainforest floor. That's exactly the point. Its color warns every predator: I'm toxic. Don't even try.
home: Strawberry poison frogs live in humid lowland rainforests from Nicaragua to Panama, hopping through leaf litter by day. In Panama's Bocas del Toro islands, isolated populations evolved into more than a dozen color forms, from red with blue legs to green, orange and yellow.
anatomy:
The strawberry poison frog is tiny, around the size of a thumbnail. In many populations it is bright red with blue or black legs, but in the islands of Bocas del Toro, Panama, it comes in more than 15 colour forms: red, orange, yellow, green, blue and spotted.

Bright colours warn predators of the alkaloid toxins in glands in its skin. Strongly coloured populations tend to be more toxic and bolder, while duller ones are more secretive. The frog has small pads on its toes for climbing among leaves.

It is active by day and has good colour vision, which matters because frogs use colour to recognise mates of their own population. Its toxins are not produced by the frog but taken from mites and ants it eats and stored in its skin.
life:
These frogs eat ants and mites. The poison on their skin, called alkaloids, comes from these prey, so frogs raised in captivity on other insects aren't toxic.

Males call from perches to defend territories, and parents share the work of raising their young.
family:
Male strawberry poison frogs defend small territories on the forest floor, calling with a buzzing chirp. After mating, the female lays a handful of eggs, often three to five, in a moist spot on a leaf. The male guards them and keeps them moist, sometimes by carrying water.

When the tadpoles hatch, the mother returns and carries each one on her back up into the trees, placing it alone in a small pool of water held in a bromeliad or other plant. Over the next weeks she visits each tadpole every few days and lays unfertilised eggs into the pool for it to eat. These eggs may pass on some of her toxins.

After about six to eight weeks, the tadpole turns into a tiny frog and climbs out.
remarkable:
After the eggs hatch, the mother carries each tadpole on her back up into the trees, placing it in its own tiny pool of water cupped in a bromeliad leaf.

Then she returns every few days to lay unfertilised eggs for it to eat. Few frogs work so hard for their young.
outlook:
The species is still common, but its forests are being cleared for farming and development, and some island color forms have tiny ranges.

Collecting for the pet trade is another pressure. Like all amphibians, it's also threatened by the deadly chytrid fungus.
people:
Strawberry poison frogs belong to the family of poison dart frogs. Some members of that family, a few species from Colombia, have toxins strong enough that the Emberá, an Indigenous people of Colombia and Panama, used them on blowgun darts, giving the family its name, though the strawberry poison frog itself was not used this way.

Because of their colours, these frogs are popular in the pet trade, and wild collection has threatened some island populations; today many are bred in captivity. Scientists study the Bocas del Toro populations to understand how new colours and species evolve, how toxins are gathered from food, and how frog parents care for their young.

Compounds from poison frogs have inspired research into new painkillers. Tourists can see them in reserves such as Red Frog Beach in Bocas del Toro, which is named after them.
relatives:
The strawberry poison frog belongs to the poison dart frogs, family Dendrobatidae, a group of around 200 species found in Central and South America. Not all are brightly coloured or toxic; many are brown and harmless. The most toxic, the golden poison frog of Colombia, carries enough toxin to kill several people.

The strawberry poison frog's genus, Oophaga, means 'egg-eater', referring to the tadpoles' diet of unfertilised eggs, a habit shared by its closest relatives, such as the harlequin poison frog. Bright warning colours and the ability to store toxins from food evolved several times within the family. Its many colour forms in Bocas del Toro arose as islands were cut off by rising sea levels several thousand years ago.
didYouKnow: The red-and-blue form is nicknamed the 'blue jeans' frog because its legs look like it's wearing denim.

quiz.prompt: Where does the frog's poison come from?
choices: The ants and mites it eats
It's born with it, whatever it eats
quiz.explanation: Toxins come from its diet; captive frogs fed other insects are harmless.

quiz.prompt: What does the mother feed her tadpoles?
choices: Nothing; they find their own food
quiz.explanation: She returns to each tadpole to lay unfertilised eggs as food.

quiz.prompt: Where are the tadpoles raised?
choices: In tiny pools held by bromeliad leaves
In the ocean, drifting with the currents
Inside the father's mouth until they turn into frogs
quiz.explanation: The mother carries each tadpole up to its own little bromeliad pool.

charities.name: Amphibian Ark
charities.blurb: Coordinates rescue and conservation breeding for amphibians facing extinction.

name: Brown-throated Sloth
range: Rainforests from Honduras to Bolivia and northern Argentina
tagline: A slow life, perfectly lived
lede: The brown-throated sloth moves so slowly that algae grows in its fur. It's not lazy; it's efficient. Living on a diet of leaves that provides very little energy, the sloth has turned slowness into a survival strategy that has worked for millions of years.
home: These three-toed sloths live in the rainforests of Central and South America, from Honduras to Bolivia. They spend almost their whole lives hanging upside-down in the canopy, gripping branches with long, curved claws.
anatomy:
The brown-throated sloth has a round head, a flat face with a dark mask across its eyes, and, as its name says, a brown throat. Its shaggy, greyish-brown fur grows in the opposite direction to most mammals', parting along the belly and running toward the back, so rain runs off while it hangs upside-down.

Each hair has cracks in which algae grow. It has three long, curved claws on each limb, up to about 10 centimetres, that hook over branches so firmly that sloths can hang, and even sleep, with little effort; some have been found still hanging after death.

It has roughly 30 percent less muscle than you would expect for an animal its size, which reduces its energy needs. Its body temperature changes with the weather more than most mammals', falling at night and rising as it basks in the morning sun.
life:
Sloths eat leaves, especially from cecropia trees. Their large, multi-chambered stomach can take weeks to digest a meal.

To save energy they move slowly, sleep a lot and let their body temperature drop at night. About once a week, they climb all the way down to the ground to poop.
family:
Brown-throated sloths live alone, each with a home range of a few trees. Females call with a shrill, high-pitched scream, a sound like 'ay-ee', to attract males when ready to mate.

After a pregnancy of about six months, the female gives birth to a single baby while hanging in the trees. The baby clings to her belly and travels with her for around six months, learning which leaves to eat by licking them from her lips. As it grows, it begins to eat on its own.

When it leaves, the mother often hands over part of her home range to her offspring, and young sloths may stay nearby. Sloths grow slowly and reach maturity at around three years. In the wild, their main predators are harpy eagles, jaguars and ocelots.
remarkable:
Green algae grow in grooves in sloth hair, helping them blend into the treetops, and moths live in their fur too.

Three-toed sloths have extra neck bones, letting them turn their heads about 270 degrees. Surprisingly, they are good swimmers.
outlook: The brown-throated sloth is still widespread, but deforestation breaks up its forest, forcing sloths onto the ground, roads and power lines where they're in danger. Wildlife bridges and power-line insulation in Costa Rica are helping them get around safely.
people:
Sloths have long puzzled and charmed people. Early European naturalists described them as lazy and badly designed, an idea scientists have since overturned: they are superbly adapted to a low-energy life.

In recent years, sloths have become internet stars, and sanctuaries in Costa Rica and Panama care for orphaned and injured sloths, many hurt by power lines, dogs or traffic. Conservation groups build rope 'sloth crossings' over roads, insulate power lines and plant trees to reconnect forest patches.

The pet trade is a growing problem, as people pay to take selfies with captive sloths, which can be stressful for these shy animals. Tourists can help by choosing responsible wildlife experiences that do not involve holding sloths. Scientists also study sloth fur, which hosts unique fungi and microbes that may lead to new medicines.
relatives:
There are six living species of sloth in two groups: the three-toed sloths, including the brown-throated, pale-throated, maned and pygmy three-toed sloth, and the two-toed sloths. The two groups are not as close as they look; they evolved tree-hanging habits separately from different ground-living ancestors.

Sloths are related to anteaters and, more distantly, armadillos, together forming a group of mammals that evolved in South America. Their ancestors include giant ground sloths such as Megatherium, which was as big as an elephant and could stand on its hind legs, and lived until about 10,000 years ago.

Ground sloths reached North America too, and their bones have been found in Yukon caves. The pygmy three-toed sloth lives only on a single island off Panama and is critically endangered.
didYouKnow: A sloth's slow movements make it hard for eagles and jaguars, which hunt by spotting motion, to notice them.

quiz.prompt: Why does a sloth's fur often look green?
choices: It's dyed by the fruit it eats
quiz.explanation: Algae grows in grooves in the hair and helps with camouflage.

quiz.prompt: How often do sloths climb down to the ground?
choices: About once a week, to poop
quiz.explanation: They descend roughly once a week to relieve themselves.

quiz.prompt: Why do sloths move so slowly?
choices: Their leafy diet gives them very little energy
They're always sleepy from fermenting fruit
quiz.explanation: Slow movement saves energy on a low-calorie diet of leaves.

charities.name: The Sloth Conservation Foundation
charities.blurb: Builds wildlife bridges and researches sloths in Costa Rica.

name: Jaguar
range: From northern Mexico through the Amazon to northern Argentina
tagline: The water-loving king of the Americas
lede: The jaguar is the largest cat in the Americas and the third largest in the world. Unlike most cats, it loves water. In Brazil's Pantanal wetlands, jaguars swim rivers, hunt caimans and fish, and doze on sandbanks in the afternoon heat.
home: Jaguars live in rainforests, swamps, grasslands and dry forests from Mexico to Argentina, with strongholds in the Amazon and the Pantanal. They prefer to stay close to rivers and lakes, and they need large connected areas of wild land.
anatomy:
The jaguar is a stocky, muscular cat with a broad head, powerful jaws and short, thick legs, built for strength rather than long chases. Its golden coat is covered in black rosettes, most with one or more dots in the centre, and some jaguars are almost entirely black, a colour form called melanistic, though their rosettes still show in sunlight.

Its canine teeth are long and its bite force exceptional for its size, strong enough to pierce turtle shells and the thick skulls of caimans. Large paws with sharp, retractable claws help it grip prey and climb trees.

Jaguars have excellent night vision and hearing, and are confident swimmers with a stocky build suited to wading through wetlands. Their call is a deep, repeated grunt, often compared to the sound of a saw cutting wood.
life: Jaguars eat almost anything they can catch: capybaras, deer, peccaries, caimans, turtles, fish and even anacondas. They usually hunt alone at dawn and dusk, stalking quietly and ambushing prey. Females raise their cubs for about two years.
family:
Jaguars are solitary. Males have large territories that may overlap with those of several females, and both sexes mark their areas with scratches, urine and scent. When a female is ready to breed, she calls more often to attract males, and the pair stays together for a few days.

After about three and a half months, she gives birth in a den, often among rocks, dense vegetation or a riverbank cave, to usually one to four cubs, which are blind at first. They begin to follow her at around two months and learn to hunt by watching and practising.

Cubs stay with their mother for about two years before leaving to establish their own territories. Young males often travel far, and this is when many come into conflict with people.
remarkable:
For its size, the jaguar has one of the most powerful bites of any big cat.

Instead of going for the throat, it often kills with a single bite through the skull, and can crack a turtle's shell. Its rosettes have dots inside them, which leopards' rosettes lack.
outlook:
Jaguars are near threatened and have already vanished from about half of their original range.

Forest clearing for ranching and farming, fires, and conflict with cattle ranchers are the biggest threats. Wildlife corridors connecting protected areas are key to their future.
people:
The jaguar was a powerful symbol for many civilisations of the Americas. The Olmec, Maya and Aztecs linked it to royalty, warfare and the underworld; Aztec elite warriors were known as jaguar warriors, and Maya rulers wore jaguar skins.

In the 20th century, jaguars were heavily hunted for their fur, until international trade was banned in the 1970s. Today they are threatened by deforestation and by ranchers who kill them for preying on cattle.

Conservation groups such as Panthera work with ranchers to protect herds using better fencing, guard animals and compensation, and promote jaguar tourism, especially in Brazil's Pantanal, where visitors can see them hunting along rivers. The Jaguar Corridor Initiative aims to keep populations connected from Mexico to Argentina, and jaguars occasionally still wander into the southern United States.
relatives:
The jaguar is the only living Panthera species in the Americas, and its closest relatives are the leopard and the lion. Its ancestors crossed from Asia into North America over the Bering land bridge around 1.5 million years ago.

During the ice ages, jaguars were larger and lived as far north as the central United States, and the American lion, a relative of today's lion, also roamed North America. Jaguars survived the extinctions at the end of the last ice age that wiped out many large mammals.

Although they look like leopards, jaguars are stockier, with a larger head and shorter tail. Black jaguars are not a separate species; they carry a gene that produces extra dark pigment, as do black leopards, which are often called black panthers.
didYouKnow: The name 'jaguar' is often traced to yaguara, a word from the Tupi-Guarani languages of Indigenous South America, said to mean something like 'one who kills with a single leap'.

quiz.prompt: How can you tell a jaguar from a leopard?
choices: Jaguar rosettes have spots inside them
Jaguars have stripes on their legs and back
Leopards are always bigger and heavier than jaguars
quiz.explanation: Jaguar rosettes usually contain small dots; leopard rosettes don't.

quiz.prompt: How do jaguars often kill their prey?
choices: With a bite through the skull
By chasing it until it's exhausted
quiz.explanation: Their powerful bite can pierce skulls and turtle shells.

quiz.prompt: What do jaguars think of water?
choices: They love it and are strong swimmers
They avoid it completely and never learn to swim
They are afraid of rivers and cross them only by fallen trees
quiz.explanation: Jaguars swim well and hunt caimans and fish in rivers.

charities.name: Panthera
charities.blurb: Global wild cat conservation, including the Jaguar Corridor Initiative.

name: Andean Condor
range: The Andes mountains and Pacific coast of South America, from Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego
tagline: The bird that barely needs to flap
lede: With wings stretching more than 3 metres, the Andean condor is one of the largest flying birds in the world. It's also one of the most efficient. One tracked condor flew more than 170 kilometres over five hours without flapping its wings once.
home: Andean condors live along the Andes mountains, from Venezuela to the southern tip of South America, and along nearby Pacific coasts. They nest on high cliff ledges and soar over open grasslands and mountains in search of food.
anatomy:
The Andean condor is a huge, black vulture with white patches on its wings and a ruff of white feathers around the base of its neck. Its head and neck are bare and greyish to reddish, an advantage for a bird that feeds inside carcasses, since bare skin stays cleaner; the skin can flush or change colour with the bird's mood.

Males have a large, fleshy comb on their forehead and a wattle on their neck. Unlike most birds of prey, males are larger than females.

Its feet are relatively weak and not built for grasping, so it cannot carry prey; instead, it uses its strong, hooked beak to tear through tough hides. Its huge wings have long, separated primary feathers at the tips, which act like fingers to reduce turbulence and help it soar on rising air.
life:
Condors are scavengers. They eat carrion, mostly large dead animals like guanacos, cattle, and on the coast, dead sea lions and whales.

They help keep ecosystems clean. Pairs mate for life and raise just one chick every two years, caring for it for over a year.
family:
Andean condors usually mate for life. Courtship involves the male puffing out his neck, spreading his wings, hissing and clicking. Pairs nest on high, inaccessible cliff ledges or in caves, usually without building much of a nest, and the female lays a single egg every second year.

Both parents take turns incubating it for about two months, then feed the chick by regurgitating food. The young condor can fly at around six months, but it stays with its parents and is fed by them for up to two years.

Condors take a long time to grow up: they gain their adult colours and begin breeding at around six to eight years old. Their slow pace means that every death of an adult has a big effect on the population.
remarkable:
Condors ride rising currents of warm air and wind deflected off mountains, flapping during only about one percent of their flight time, mostly during take-off.

They can soar to over 5,000 metres. Males have a fleshy comb on their heads and a ruff of white feathers around their necks.
outlook:
Condors are vulnerable because they breed so slowly. Many are poisoned by bait set out for predators or by lead from bullets in carcasses, and some are shot.

Captive breeding and release programs have returned condors to areas where they had vanished.
people:
The Andean condor has been a sacred bird for Andean peoples for thousands of years; Inca beliefs linked it to the upper world and the heavens, and it remains a symbol of strength and freedom. It appears on the coats of arms of Bolivia, Chile, Colombia and Ecuador and in countless songs and festivals, including the famous Peruvian tune 'El Cóndor Pasa'.

Yet condors have declined, especially in the northern Andes, poisoned by baits left for pumas and foxes, by lead from bullets in carcasses, and occasionally shot. Zoos in North and South America breed condors, and since the late 1980s captive-raised birds have been released in Colombia, Venezuela, Argentina and elsewhere, often raised with condor puppets so they don't become used to humans, an approach first developed for the related California condor.
relatives:
The Andean condor is one of the New World vultures, family Cathartidae, along with the California condor, the king vulture and the turkey vulture. Despite their similar lifestyle, New World vultures are not closely related to Old World vultures of Africa, Europe and Asia, which belong to the hawk and eagle family; their bald heads and soaring flight evolved separately.

The California condor, the only other condor, came close to extinction in the 1980s, when the last 27 wild birds were captured for breeding; today several hundred fly again. Condor relatives were once much larger: Argentavis, which lived in Argentina about 6 million years ago, had a wingspan estimated at around 6 metres, making it one of the largest flying birds ever.
didYouKnow: The Andean condor is a national symbol of Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru.

quiz.prompt: What do Andean condors eat?
quiz.explanation: Condors are scavengers that feed on carcasses.

quiz.prompt: How do condors fly so efficiently?
choices: They soar on rising air and rarely flap
They flap very fast, like a hummingbird, to stay up
They ride in the slipstream of flocks of other birds
quiz.explanation: Condors flap only about one percent of the time, riding air currents.

quiz.prompt: How often do condors raise a chick?
choices: About one chick every two years
Twice a year, after the rains in spring and autumn
Only once in their lives, at about 50 years old
quiz.explanation: Their slow breeding makes populations vulnerable to losses.
